newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council backs Croatia plan for Eastern Slavonia.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council backs Croatia plan for Eastern Slavonia.

text.p: The Security Council has given Croatia a green light for holding elections in its Eastern Slavonia enclave and called on Serbs to accept key concessions Zagreb offered two weeks ago.
The once-volatile region, dominated by Serbs and bordering the Yugoslav republic of Serbia, is the only remaining Croatian area not under Zagreb's control.

A U.N. Transitional Authority, known as UNTAES, has been administering the enclave for over a year to prevent any resumption of fighting between Belgrade and Zagreb before the region is returned to Croatia.

In a statement read at a formal meeting on Friday, the council said that Zagreb's guarantees to Serbs, negotiated at length with the United Nations, constituted a "solid basis" for holding elections, tentatively scheduled for March 16.
"The council underlines the need for full cooperation by the local Serbs," said the statement, which at the same time warned Croatia to "implement fully" its commitments.

Croatia has promised citizenship to Serbs living in the area since January 1996, Serb representation at various levels of local, and national government bodies, access to social services and educational and cultural autonomy.
In addition, the Serbs in Eastern Slavonia are exempt from military service for two years and can apply for conscientious objector status after that.
Serb leaders in the enclave, despite urging from Jacques Klein, the American diplomat in charge of the region for the United Nations, have protested Croatia's promises.

They want permanent demilitarization of the enclave, exemption from military service for at least 15 years, guarantees to remain in their present homes until their original houses are rebuilt and the creation of a separate political "county" for the region.

Croatia outlined the guarantees in a January 13 letter to the United Nations that was also welcomed by State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns in Washington. He called it "significant" and a "substantial steap forward for the situation in Eastern Slavonia."

The 5,000 U.N. troops are to begin leaving Croatia 30 days after the elections and be gone by July 1. After that civilian monitors and some military observers are expected to remain for at least another six months.

There are anywhere between 110,000 and 140,000 Serbs in Eastern Slavonia, many of whom fled from other Serb-dominated areas of Croatia during Zagreb's military offensive in the summer of 1995. Croatia says about 56,000 have applied for documents and about 46,000 have been issued.
Klein told reporters it was necessary the council send a "clear signal" to the Serbs. "They don't like the idea of living in Croatia. I understand that, but at the same time we have to move forward."

The council also encouraged Croatia to maintain the current demilitarized status of the region but it failed to approve Klein's proposal that Serbia should do likewise in some areas on its side of the border, diplomats said.

Klein, at times by the sheer force of his personality, is credited with making inroads in the Serb population, such as organising as recruiting police to serve with Croatia police, starting programmes to reunite families and driving corrupt Serb militias from the enclave and its oil fields.

As the council was deliberating a Belgian UNTAES soldier was killed in Vukovar and other others were injured. But U.N. officials say it appeared to be the act of a single individual. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, the United States and the Security Council condemned the incident.
